summaries.example: Imagine two students answer a science question correctly. One guessed. The other looked carefully, remembered what they learned, and checked the evidence. Virtue epistemology says the second student’s answer shows better thinking because the truth came from good thinking abilities and habits, not just luck.
summaries.summary: Virtue epistemology is a group of philosophical approaches about knowledge and good thinking. It treats epistemology as a subject about what we should believe, how we should investigate, and what makes thinking excellent. Instead of looking only at whether a belief is true, it also looks at the thinker: Did the person use good abilities or habits? Did the answer come from care, memory, perception, curiosity, or open-mindedness? Or did it come from haste, prejudice, or luck? Some philosophers focus on natural abilities, called faculty-virtues. Others focus on learned character traits, called trait-virtues. Many think both kinds may matter. A common idea is that knowledge is true belief that comes from intellectual virtue. This helps explain why a lucky guess does not seem as good as an answer reached through skill. It also helps explain why knowledge may be more valuable than merely having a true belief. Still, philosophers disagree. They debate whether people deserve credit for knowledge learned from other people, whether knowledge depends on the situation, and whether human thinking is reliable enough to count as virtuous. The field also studies understanding, wisdom, intellectual emotions, and the virtues of communities.
key_ideas: Virtue epistemology studies good and bad ways of thinking, not only separate beliefs.
Many virtue epistemologists say knowledge is true belief produced by intellectual ability or virtue.
Some emphasize abilities such as memory and vision; others emphasize learned traits such as honesty, patience, and open-mindedness.
Knowledge often depends on other people, teams, schools, tools, and communities.
Philosophers disagree about how virtues work, how much luck matters, and whether knowledge changes with context.
summaries.why_it_matters: We constantly decide what to believe, whom to trust, and when to check information. Thinking about intellectual virtues can encourage curiosity, honesty, patience, humility, and fair listening. It also reminds us that good knowing is often social: teachers, friends, libraries, tools, and communities can help us learn. The approach does not give one simple answer to every question, but it gives us useful ways to notice both good thinking and thinking that can lead us astray.

important_terms.definition: The study of knowledge: what it is, how we get it, and when beliefs are reasonable.
A good thinking ability or habit that helps someone understand things well, such as carefulness, curiosity, or open-mindedness.
A thinking habit or ability that makes inquiry go badly, such as rushing, closed-mindedness, or carelessness.
A belief or answer that is true because it came from someone’s good thinking ability, rather than from a lucky guess.
A rule or value about how people ought to think, investigate, and share information.
The people and groups who help create, check, and pass along knowledge.

questions_to_think_about: Is being right enough, or does it matter how someone reached the right answer?
Can a person have a good memory but still be a poor thinker?
How can a group help its members avoid mistakes?
When should we slow down and check a belief?
Can asking questions and admitting limits be signs of strength?

summaries.example: Suppose a student identifies a tree correctly by using field marks, comparing several reliable sources, and noticing uncertainty about the species. Another student gives the same answer after a lucky guess. A virtue epistemologist may say the first has an achievement: the true belief is accurate because it manifests competence. But the case becomes harder if the student learned the answer from a trustworthy expert, or if the environment contained many misleading look-alike trees. Those details raise questions about credit, testimony, and epistemic luck.
summaries.summary: Virtue epistemology is a diverse research program united by two broad commitments. First, epistemology is normative: it concerns norms, values, duties, and standards for belief and inquiry, although empirical psychology and related sciences can help determine what human cognition can achieve. Second, epistemic evaluation should focus on intellectual agents and communities, including the traits and abilities expressed in their cognitive performances. This produces a virtue-theoretic direction of analysis: the epistemic status of a belief or inquiry is explained partly by the qualities of the cognizer, much as virtue ethics explains an action partly by the agent’s character. The field divides over the nature of virtue. Virtue reliabilists emphasize faculties such as perception, memory, and intuition. Virtue responsibilists emphasize cultivated traits such as conscientiousness, courage, humility, and open-mindedness. The source presents this division as contested, since both abilities and traits may contribute to knowledge, understanding, and wisdom. A central proposal is that knowledge is true belief because of intellectual virtue or competence. This proposal aims to explain why knowledge excludes certain kinds of luck, why Gettier cases fail to be knowledge, and why knowledge is more valuable than accidental true belief: knowing is an achievement for which the knower receives credit. Objections concern fake-barn cases, testimonial knowledge, innate knowledge, and whether credit must mean praise, authorship, or shared contribution. Virtue epistemology also includes contextualist theories, empirical challenges about unstable human reasoning, and approaches that locate cognitive support in social, material, and technological environments. key_ideas: Virtue epistemology is normative: it asks how inquiry and belief ought to be evaluated, while remaining open to empirical research on cognition.
Its central focus is the intellectual agent or community and the virtues and vices expressed in cognitive performances.
A major division contrasts faculty-virtues with cultivated trait-virtues, though the source notes that a complete theory may need both.
Many accounts connect knowledge with true belief produced through competence, achievement, or credit; critics question how these ideas handle testimony, luck, and Gettier cases.
Conventional approaches analyze knowledge and justification, while alternative approaches emphasize inquiry, understanding, wisdom, education, social cognition, and intellectual culture.
Situationist research and work on epistemic communities suggest that environments, institutions, tools, and other people may support or undermine intellectual virtue.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry connects abstract theories of knowledge with practical questions about inquiry. It asks what makes research careful, what makes testimony trustworthy, how communities can transmit knowledge, and how people can respond to bias and cognitive limitation. It also shows why being correct is not always enough: the route to truth, the role of ability, the influence of luck, and the contribution of others can all affect epistemic evaluation. Studying these issues can clarify education, research, disagreement, public reasoning, and the cultivation of intellectual character.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of knowledge, belief, evidence, justification, and related forms of epistemic evaluation.
A characteristic that promotes intellectual flourishing or makes for an excellent cognizer; theories differ about whether it is a faculty, a cultivated trait, or both.
A defect or disposition that obstructs effective and responsible inquiry, such as closed-mindedness, wishful thinking, or indifference to truth.
A theory that treats abilities such as perception, memory, or intuition as intellectual virtues, especially when they reliably produce success.
A theory that emphasizes cultivated traits such as conscientiousness, intellectual courage, humility, or open-mindedness.
The idea that knowledge is true belief formed because of intellectual competence or virtue, rather than being true merely by accident.
A problem about whether knowledge-attributions change with conversational context, interests, or standards of explanation.
A challenge claiming that seemingly irrelevant situational factors can strongly affect people’s thinking, making intellectual virtue difficult to identify.

questions_to_think_about: Does a person deserve epistemic credit when a true belief mainly comes from someone else’s testimony?
Can a belief be knowledge if the ability producing it is unreliable in the surrounding environment?
Should epistemology focus mainly on defining knowledge, or also on improving inquiry and education?
How might a community correct biases that an individual cannot notice alone?
Is intellectual humility mainly a belief about one’s limits, an emotion, a practice, or some combination?

summaries.example: A student hears a rumor that school will close. She could repeat it immediately, but instead asks where it came from, checks the school’s message, listens to a trusted adult, and stays willing to change her mind. If the rumor turns out to be false, her careful process still shows intellectual virtues. If it turns out to be true, her belief is better than a lucky guess because it came from checking evidence and using good judgment.
summaries.summary: Virtue epistemology is a family of theories about knowledge that puts the thinker at the center. It asks what good thinking looks like and what makes a belief or investigation successful in a way that is not merely lucky. The field views epistemology as normative, meaning that it studies standards about how people should form beliefs, seek evidence, ask questions, and respond to disagreement. It also studies groups and communities, because people often gain and share knowledge together. Intellectual virtues are qualities that help someone think well. Some philosophers emphasize faculty-virtues, such as accurate perception, strong memory, or useful intuition. Others emphasize trait-virtues, such as open-mindedness, conscientiousness, intellectual courage, and humility. The source explains that this division is not always sharp: a full account might need both abilities and learned character. Many virtue epistemologists offer a special account of knowledge. In broad terms, knowledge is true belief that comes from intellectual virtue or competence. This is meant to explain why a lucky true guess is not knowledge and why knowledge may be more valuable than a true belief that happened accidentally. It is also used to discuss Gettier cases, in which a belief seems justified and true but still falls short of knowledge because of unusual luck. Critics raise challenges involving misleading environments, testimony, and beliefs that depend heavily on other people. The entry also discusses contextualism, which says that knowledge claims may vary with context, and situationism, which examines evidence that mood, social pressure, and other ordinary conditions can affect reasoning. key_ideas: Virtue epistemology asks not only whether a belief is true, but also whether it was formed through good thinking.
It has two main tendencies: studying norms for belief and focusing on thinkers, their traits, and their communities.
Philosophers disagree about whether intellectual virtues are mainly natural abilities, learned traits, or both.
A popular account says knowledge is true belief produced by competence, which helps explain why luck can undermine knowledge.
Some approaches study classic puzzles about knowledge; others focus on education, inquiry, wisdom, misinformation, and social life.
Human thinking can be supported by communities, institutions, information tools, and well-designed environments.
summaries.why_it_matters: This philosophy helps explain everyday choices about rumors, online information, disagreement, and trust. It encourages people to ask not only, “Was the answer right?” but also, “How was it reached?” and “Did the thinker respond responsibly to evidence?” It also challenges the idea that knowing is always a solo activity. Teachers, friends, experts, libraries, technologies, and fair communities can all help people think better, while biased or careless environments can make knowledge harder to obtain.

important_terms.definition: The study of knowledge and of what makes beliefs, evidence, and inquiry good or bad.
A quality that helps a person think, learn, and investigate well, such as curiosity, honesty, carefulness, or open-mindedness.
A habit or attitude that gets in the way of responsible thinking, such as rushing to judgment or refusing evidence.
A view that treats reliable abilities, such as memory or perception, as important intellectual virtues.
A view that treats learned character traits, such as intellectual courage or conscientiousness, as important intellectual virtues.
The idea that knowledge is not just a true belief; it is a true belief reached through the thinker’s ability or virtue.
The idea that what counts as knowing may depend partly on the situation, the speaker’s purposes, or the standards being used.
The idea that ordinary situations can influence thinking so much that people’s intellectual habits may not be as steady as we assume.

questions_to_think_about: If you get the right answer by guessing, have you shown knowledge?
Can someone be intellectually virtuous while admitting, “I do not know”?
Which matters more in a group project: individual skill or cooperation?
How might a stressful situation change someone’s judgment?
Should schools teach intellectual virtues directly, or mainly teach facts and methods?
